Read this conversation between an aged mother and her caregiver in an old age home. Ritu (caregiver) : Good morning, Sudha auntie! How are you today? Ms Sudha : (sighs) Just another day, dear. Another day without my family. Ritu : I’m so sorry, auntie. I know it’s hard. How can I help you? Can you tell me more about what’s on your mind? Ms Sudha : You know they brought me here and left. It is a long story, dear. My children told me that they couldn’t take care of me any more. Ritu : Auntie… I understand your feelings. Ms Sudha : Understand? No! Nobody understands me. I sacrificed my life for my kids and here I am…all alone. Ritu : Oh! I know you’re suffering, auntie. But, you’re loved and valued here. Consider us your new family. Ms Sudha : Do you really care?

You are just doing your job, aren't you? Ritu : No, auntie. We are here to love you and to listen to your stories and experiences. You will never be alone again, never. This conversation highlights the emotional state of elderly individuals who may feel that there is nothing left in life. It also underscores the rising need for empathetic caregivers. Prepare a short script for a skit to be performed in your class, based on the above conversation.

2. Read the following excerpt from the memoir. On 12 December, the officer came for the last time. He brought me a larger supply of bread than before and a warm eiderdown. Who knows what may happen? You have a long way to go home. If I survive, I’ll certainly be working for Polish Radio again. I was there before the war.

If anything happens to you, if I can help you then in any way, remember my name: Szpilman, Polish Radio.” He smiled his usual smile, half shy and embarrassed, but I felt I had given him pleasure with my naive wish to help him.

3. ‘In the Attic’ highlights the human experience of displacement and survival in times of war and persecution. Read this post which appeared on social media on the occasion of World Refugee Day. The global refugee crisis is one of humanity’s most pressing issues with millions displaced due to conflict, persecution, and natural disasters. According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), over 80 million people have been displaced worldwide in recent years, with nearly 26 million refugees seeking safety outside their country of origin. Refugees have to face an uncertain future and are usually denied basic necessities such as food, shelter and healthcare. In this context, concerns regarding the policies of various countries and the distribution of humanitarian aid are among the world’s most pressing issues today.

CLASS X UNIT - I 5. Read this excerpt from a letter by E. Moshe, who died in the Warsaw ghetto, to his daughter Ola. Wednesday (April 1943) My darling! I am holding fast. What will be afterwards – God only knows. Whatever happens – don't be sorry. I am no more worthy than so many brothers and sisters. Either way, I hope to get to a safe haven. I only think about and worry for your fate. You, my darling Ola, on your shoulders rest the responsibility to take care of your mother and sisters. I tried to be brave and arrange everything calmly and wisely. That was the only thing that could save you. Of course, I am writing this with the sense of responsibility of a father and husband. I have not for one moment lost hope that I will be saved and return to you. It is very bad for me that I was left penniless. It makes it very hard to get food. And if you have a chance to escape, remember it is impossible without money.…

Note the impact of war on Moshe’s family. Displacement, separation and emotional trauma are the inevitable consequences of war for most families. Shall we conduct a poster exhibition as part of an anti-war campaign to raise awareness about the devastating effects of war and the importance of promoting peace?

He is assassinated in the Capitol by a band of conspirators, led by his bosom friend Brutus. CLASS X UNIT - II Don’t you want to know the rest of the story? Do you want to know more about Bablu's journey? Here is his story in his own words. Interview with Padma Shri Arunachalam Muruganantham, the ‘Pad Man’ of India, ('Bablu' in Twinkle Khanna’s story).

Good morning, Mr Muruganantham, it's very kind of you to meet and talk to us. We know that you've been working on the manufacture and distribution of inexpensive sanitary napkins for a quarter of a century. Now, we'd like to learn about your early days. Did anyone inspire you to work for the good of the community? Good morning friends. Let me, at the outset, tell you my story. My father was a handloom weaver. I dropped out of school at 14 when he passed away quite unexpectedly. My mother worked on a farm, and she found it very difficult to make ends meet. She had to take care of two daughters and a son, you know. She had hoped I’d become an engineer. However, she couldn’t afford to send me to college, and I had to take up a job in a welding workshop, even as a young boy. At 21, I married. It was then I discovered that my wife, Shanti, had to use old rags instead of clean napkins during her menstrual cycle.

This made me think about the general state of women’s health and hygiene. The knowledge triggered my research into the manufacture of affordable napkins.  We understand that it took you years to find the right materials for your napkins. Could you tell us more about that phase of your research? As I mentioned earlier, my father was a weaver. Therefore, I was somewhat familiar with cotton, and made use of many varieties of cotton. All my initial experiments failed miserably. Moreover, the topic was taboo in our village at the time, and my interest in the subject led to my isolation within the community and even my family. But I didn't give up.

I tried to find out what type of cotton the popular brands were using for their napkins. It took me two years of trial and error to figure out it was pinewood pulp and not cotton. The suppliers sent me some samples. I spent several days wondering how to make cellulose from it. One day, my pet dog accidentally scratched the sample card, and I could see the soft cottony material. This gave me the idea of defibration.  Later, Mr Muruganantham, you discovered that the real need was for more efficient machinery. How did you understand this? The machines that produced sanitary napkins cost crores at the time. I realised that women would get affordable napkins only if the machinery became less expensive. I then began to focus on designing affordable machines. Again, by trial and error, I succeeded in designing and building relatively inexpensive machines. These could be operated by people without much training.

I designed three separate machines for the defibration, compression, and sterilisation of the material. This too is the result of trial and error, the only method I’d ever recommend for genuine innovation.  Sir, of course, many MNCs would have made you handsome offers for your machines. Were you ever tempted to take any of these offers? It took me thirteen years to get a patent for my invention. When I got the patent, I placed it in the public domain, for anyone who wanted to use it. I sell my machines at a subsidised price to women’s self-help groups. My profit margin is based on need, not greed. I believe that the success of entrepreneurship lies not in making money, but in allowing others to benefit.  Sir, why do you promote women and women’s self-help groups so much? Gandhiji strongly believed that women could transform India. I follow Gandhiji's wisdom and his path.

My vision is to generate one million jobs for women in India and to promote one hundred per cent hygiene in households. How can I best do that? I use the power of women to empower women. In my mission, three elements are the most important ones awareness, availability, and affordability. Women can communicate effectively with women, and create awareness on menstrual hygiene.

You have said that you prefer to use the word ‘detail’ rather than ‘retail’ when you mention your product. Could you explain what you mean by this? More than turnover, I focus on impact. Social entrepreneurship should be impact-based. I ask the women’s collectives to personally talk to every woman customer in detail about hygiene. Our aim is not to increase sales but to increase awareness. We have created 1363 local brands and earned three-quarters of a billion dollars in revenue so far. Detailing information and creating awareness is a tough thing to do. I bow to all teachers as they spend their whole lives detailing things to pupils.  Did you ever get any support from policymakers or government agencies for your project, sir? Can you tell us how the government supported your efforts?

IIT Madras honoured me with the National Innovation Foundation’s ‘Grassroots Technological Innovations Award.’ I received the award from President of India. The Government of India selected me for the Padma Shri award in 2016. The Indian Parliament discussed the issue of women health and hygiene at great length, and the government waived GST on sanitary napkins. But what I consider the most important of all is that my family came back to me.  What message do you have specifically for the young innovators and social entrepreneurs of our nation? What advice would you give to students? Education empowers us. We must, however, always bear in mind that we do not need to beg for a job after education. Try to find solutions to social problems and create jobs for yourselves and others. You need education and knowledge to identify the problems. Convert every problem into an opportunity.

Come out with a solution, an invention, an innovation, an enterprise. Become solution providers and social entrepreneurs. Transform the world. Thank you very much, sir. We're sure your life and your words of wisdom will indeed be an inspiration for generations to come.

The Seedling - Paul Laurence Dunbar As a quiet little seedling Lay within its darksome bed, To itself it fell a-talking, And this is what it said: “I am not so very robust, But I’ll do the best I can;” And the seedling from that moment Its work of life began. So it pushed a little leaflet Up into the light of day, To examine the surroundings And show the rest the way. The leaflet liked the prospect, So it called its brother, Stem; Then two other leaflets heard it, And quickly followed them.

CLASS X UNIT - II To be sure, the haste and hurry Made the seedling sweat and pant; But almost before it knew it It found itself a plant. The sunshine poured upon it, And the clouds they gave a shower; And the little plant kept growing Till it found itself a flower. Little folks, be like the seedling, Always do the best you can; Every child must share life’s labour Just as well as every man. And the sun and showers will help you Through the lonesome, struggling hours, Till you raise to light and beauty Virtue’s fair, unfading flowers.

Connecting words like either...or and neither...nor are conjunctions.

Either... or and neither...nor are pairs of conjunctions. They correlate words, phrases or clauses of equal importance. Her style is influenced by the rhythms of oral African literature. Diome lectures at Marc Bloch University, Strasbourg, and at the Institute of Pedagogy of Karlsruhe (Germany). She presents cultural and literary television programmes on French television. She lives in Strasbourg, France.

Let’s perform a Radio Play • Shall we transform Fatou Diome’s Préférence Nationale into a radio play, capturing the social criticism, the emotional depth, and the satire in the story? Let’s begin by exploring the Key Features of a Radio Play:

1. Characters • Each character must have a distinct voice and personality. Their emotions need to be conveyed through tone, pitch, and pace as there is no scope for body language or facial expressions. 2. Narration • The narrator provides the background, reveals the transitions between scenes, and expresses the protagonist’s thoughts. The narration must be engaging and well-paced. 3. Dialogue and Monologues • These drive the story forward, revealing the personalities of the characters and their relationships. Voice modulation is essential—characters should pause, hesitate, sigh, or raise their voice, in the most natural manner. 4. Sound Effects (SFX) and Music • SFX create realism: footsteps, door creaks, street noise, a telephone ringing. • Music sets the mood: melancholic piano notes to indicate disappointment, tense strings for confrontation. 5.
Expressive Voice Acting • Since radio plays lack visuals, actors must rely on vocal expression to convey emotions.

Let's read and enjoy: Have you ever looked into a mirror and wondered who you truly are beneath the surface? What happens when the reflection staring back at you is not just a silent observer but a witness to your deepest secrets. Here is a poem that explores how a mirror image shape the person we see and the one we struggle to accept. Mirror - Sylvia Plath I am silver and exact. I have no preconceptions. Whatever I see I swallow immediately Just as it is, unmisted by love or dislike. I am not cruel, only truthful‚ The eye of a little god, four-cornered. Most of the time I meditate on the opposite wall. It is pink, with speckles. I have looked at it so long I think it is part of my heart. But it flickers. Faces and darkness separate us over and over.

Now I am a lake. A woman bends over me, Searching my reaches for what she really is. Then she turns to those liars, the candles or the moon. I see her back, and reflect it faithfully. She rewards me with tears and an agitation of hands. I am important to her. She comes and goes. Each morning it is her face that replaces the darkness. In me she has drowned a young girl, and in me an old woman Rises toward her day after day, like a terrible fish.

About the poet Sylvia Plath (1932 – 1963) was an American poet, novelist, and writer of short stories. She was born in Boston, Massachusetts. Her most notable contributions are in the genre of confessional poetry. She is one of the best- known writers of the 20th century. She published a collection of poems in her lifetime, The Colossus (1960), and a semi-autobiographical novel, The Bell Jar (1963). She won a posthumous Pulitzer Prize for Poetry in 1982 for The Collected Poems, published in 1981, almost 20 years after her death.

A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings: At a Glance "A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings" by Gabriel Garcia Marquez is a powerful example of magical realism, which blends the ordinary and the extraordinary in a unique and captivating narrative style. One gloomy afternoon, Pelayo saw a strange old man lying face down in the mud in his back courtyard. He had huge dirty wings. He looked weak and tired. Frightened, Pelayo and his wife Elisenda inspect the man closely. He was dressed in rags. His wings were stuck in the mud, and he could not get up. He appeared like a wet grandfather than a divine being. The old man spoke an unknown language. They assumed that he might be a shipwrecked foreigner. But a neighbour woman said that he was an angel who had come for their sick child.

The next day, the entire town flocked to their courtyard to see the angel. They treated him like a strange animal. The visitors threw food at him. Pelayo locked him in the chicken coop to keep him safe. They charged five cents as an admission fee from the visitors to see the angel. Thus, they became rich, built a beautiful house, and lived in comfort. Pilgrims and others from far away places visited the angel, hoping for miracles. But the angel remained passive and patient, ignored and mistreated by people.

The people soon lost interest in the angel when a new attraction - a woman who had been turned into a spider - arrived in the town. They stopped visiting Pelayo's house, but by that time, the couple had made enough money. As time passed, the angel was forgotten. The chicken coop became dirty and broken, and the angel grew weaker. But, then slowly he survived. New feathers grew on his wings, and he started his attempts to fly again. One day, when Elisenda was cutting onions in the kitchen, she saw the angel struggling to fly. At last, he lifted off and disappeared into the distance. She watched him until he became a mere dot on the horizon. She felt a kind of relief as the burden had finally left their lives. 2. In The Attic : At a glance

"In the Attic" is an except from Wadyslaw Szpilman's survivor testimony titled "The Pianist."It revolves around the unusual friendship between Szpilman and Captain Wilm Hosenfeld, a German officer. Szpilman was hiding in an attic during the final days of war in Warsaw. The German officer SMILE ENGLISH 3

finds him in an abandoned building and asks him to play the piano. He played Chopin's Nocturne in C- sharp minor, which moved the officer deeply. The officer offered to take Szpilman to a safer location, and it was then that he learned that Szpilman was a Jew. He told Szpilman not to stay in the city as it was dangerous. But Szpilman was not ready to leave. The officer helped him to find a better hiding place in a small loft above the attic. The officer brought him food and supplies, He admitted to the fact that he was ashamed of identifying himself as a German. He told Szpilman that the war would soon be over and that he must "hang on" to survive. Szpilman continued to live in isolation often without human contact for long intervals. The only sound heard was the artillery fire and the soldiers going up and down the stairs where he was hiding.

Before leaving the city, the officer came one last time to Szpilman and gave him extra food and a warm blanket. He advised Szpilman not to lose heart. At the parting moment Szpilman expressed his gratitude and promised to repay the officer's kindness and assistance. Szpilman survived another year there. One morning, he heard Polish announcements that the war was over and Warsaw was free. He stayed in a confused state, not knowing what to do. Then he came across the voices of women and children down the street. Excited, but cautious, he put on the German coat the officer had given him and went outside. A woman who mistook him as a German officer screamed. At that, a Polish guard shot at him, and he ran back into the attic. Later, the soldiers understood the situation, and Szpilman was rescued. For the first time in six years, he walked freely through the streets of Warsaw.

The friendship between Szpilman and the German officer remains a powerful testament to the human capacity for connection and compassion even in the most challenging circumstances. Szpilman's story is a testament to the human spirits' ability to persevere in the face of adversity.

In the story “A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings”, the writer skillfully presents the character of Pelayo through his involvement in and reactions to various events. Prepare a character sketch of Pelayo, bringing out his main traits as revealed in the story.

Pelayo, one of the central figures in the story“A Very Old Man with Enormous Wings”. Marquez portrayed him as a representative of the common man who encounters a supernatural event in the midst of his ordinary life. As a bailiff, he holds responsibility to the public, yet his foremost concern is the safety of his family. His reaction to the strange old man with wings reflects both fear and duty: startled by the unexpected sight of the winged creature trapped in the mud, his immediate instinct is to run to his wife, Elisenda, for support. Together, they approach the old man, whom they initially mistake for a shipwrecked castaway. However, when their neighbour lady interprets him as an angel who might have come for their SMILE ENGLISH 9

sick child, Pelayo’s fear deepens. That evening , he sits in his kitchen armed with his bailiff’s club, and before going to bed, he drags the old man into the chicken coop—an act that demonstrates both his anxiety and his desire to shield his loved ones.

Pelayo’s humanity is evident in his conflicting impulses. When his child is mysteriously cured, he contemplates sending the winged man back to sea with provisions. Yet, when the crowd gathers, he agrees with Elisenda’s suggestion to charge an entry fee. Although this decision reveals his willingness to profit from the situation, it also reflects his practicality as a common man struggling for survival. He uses the money wisely—resigning from his job, starting a new business, and building a comfortable new house for his family. Despite exploiting the old man for financial gain, Pelayo does not abandon his empathy and soft feelings. He allows the winged stranger to remain in his courtyard, worries about his health, and provides him with a blanket during the winter. These gestures, though modest, show his underlying kindness. Thus, Pelayo emerges as a complex character—fearful yet protective, practical yet humane.
He embodies the struggles of an ordinary man torn between survival, morality, and the mystery of the unknown.

UNIT 2 PATHS TO PROGRESS 1. BREAKING BARRIERS: I WILL FLY: At a glance This autobiographical piece tells the story of Srikanth Bolla, who was born blind. His parents were farmers in a small village in Andhra Pradesh. They accepted their son as he was and brought him up with love and care. When his father saw that Srikanth was not of much help in the fields, he decided to send him to the nearby school. At school Srikanth had to face many problems. He was made to sit on the last bench and ignored by his teachers and friends. After two years, his father sent him to a special school in Hyderabad where there were children like him. Srikanth excelled in all activities. He passed his 10th grade with 90% marks. Despite facing discrimination and rejection from the society again when he was denied admission to science stream in school—he persevered.

With an order from the government that he could study science at his own risk, he completed his 12 th grade with 98% marks. With the support of his parents and mentor, he went on to study at MIT (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) and later established a successful enterprise, Bollant Industries. The purpose of this enterprise was to rehabilitate, nurture and reintegrate disabled individuals into society. The lesson emphasizes the importance of determination, courage, and breaking societal barriers. Srikanth’s journey is a testament to how one can rise above limitations and create opportunities not just for oneself, but for others too. 2. A Phoenix Rises : At a glance This inspiring story is based on the real-life journey of Arunachalam Muruganantham, a humble man from rural Tamil Nadu who became a pioneer in menstrual hygiene. The story follows Bablu, a fictional character who mirrors Muruganantham’s life.

After the death of his father, Bablu had to drop out of school at a very early age and look for a job to help his mother who was working hard to support the family. He got a job in a workshop as a busboy. He worked hard to become a welder and gradually took over the workshop and slowly improved the business. He got married and after his marriage he noticed things that he felt required urgent attention. One day he found his wife use unhygienic cloth during her periods, Bablu was deeply disturbed. He learned that commercial sanitary pads were too expensive for poor families. Determined to help, he began experimenting with making low-cost sanitary pads.Despite being mocked, misunderstood, and abandoned by his own family, Bablu never gave up. He tested materials, built machines, and

finally discovered a way to make affordable pads using pinewood pulp. His invention not only improved women's health but also created jobs for rural women. Like a phoenix rising from the ashes, Bablu rose above rejection and humiliation to bring hope, dignity, and change to society. The story also highlights how one’s determination can remove the taboos existing in society and bring in positive changes. 3. The Seedling by Paul Laurence Dunbar Summary Paul Laurence Dunbar’s poem “The Seedling” is a gentle and inspiring piece that uses the journey of a small plant to reflect the struggles and growth of human life. The seedling, though not strong, decides to do its best and begins its journey from the dark soil to the light of day. It symbolizes human potential and the journey of growth from darkness to light. The poem conveys the message of how we must rise above challenges with courage and hope.

The poem teaches us that even if we are not perfect or powerful, we can still grow, succeed, and bloom by putting in effort and staying positive. The seedling’s determination, teamwork, and patience show us the values of hard work and self-belief. The poem uses a several poetic devices like simile “ Little folks, be like the seedling”, metaphor “ darksome bed”, personification “To itself it fell a talking,” and alliteration in “ So it pushed a little leaflet”. UNIT 3 THE TRUMPETS OF CHANGE 1. WAR : At a glance "War" by Luigi Pirandello is a short story set during World War I, on a train carrying several passengers. Most of them are parents of soldiers who are fighting or have fought in the war. Among them is a couple whose only son has just been sent to the front. The mother is heartbroken and says nothing, while the father tries to stay calm, even though he is also very sad. As the train moves, the passengers start talking about their children and the war. The conversation soon becomes a debate about duty and patriotism. One man, whose son has already died in the war, speaks strongly. He says that parents should not be selfish and cry too much, because once children grow up, they belong to their country. He believes that soldiers should go to war with pride, and parents should be proud of their sacrifice instead of feeling of pain. For a while, the other passengers seem to agree with him.

The quiet father listens to all of this, but does not speak. The passengers try to comfort themselves by thinking that their sons are dying for a noble reason—to serve their country. This idea helps them feel a little better, even if only for a short time. But then, the man who had spoken so confidently starts to show his true feelings. His voice shakes, and he becomes sad. When the grieving mother finally asks him if his son is really dead, he cannot answer right away. Then he suddenly breaks down and starts crying, realizing how much pain he truly feels. 2. A PIECE OF STRING : At a glance

The short story "A Piece of String" by Guy de Maupassant takes place in a small village named Goderville in France. The main character is an old peasant named Hauchecome. One day, while walking towards the public square, he notices a piece of string lying on the ground. Thinking it might be useful, he bends down and picks it up. Unfortunately, another man from the village, Malandain, sees him pick up the string. Hauchecome becomes ashamed to be seen thus by him. Malandain is not on good terms with Hauchecome. Hauchecome goes towards the market. Later that day, it is announced that someone has lost a pocketbook in the marketplace. The finder is requested to return the same to the Mayor’s office. When people begin to discuss the possibility of finding it, a chief of the police appears and informs Hauchecome that he is to meet the Mayor. The Mayor tells Hauchecome that he was seen picking up the lost pocketbook. Hauchecome is shocked

and tries to explain that he only picked up a piece of string. He even shows the string to prove his honesty. But no one believes him. Even after the wallet is found by someone else and returned to its owner, the villagers still think Hauchecome was involved somehow.

Despite being innocent, Hauchecome finds that people continue to treat him as if he is guilty. They mock him, whisper behind his back, and avoid him. This unfair treatment deeply affects him. He becomes obsessed with proving his innocence and keeps repeating his story to everyone he meets, hoping someone will believe him. But instead of gaining sympathy, people think he is lying even more. Over time, the stress and shame become too much for him to bear. His health worsens, and eventually, he dies, heartbroken and defeated. The story clearly shows how easily people judge others without proof and how once a person's reputation is damaged, it is very difficult to repair, even if they are truly innocent. 3. Appreciation of the song ‘Another Day in Paradise’ Phil Collins’ song ‘Another Day in Paradise’ tells the story of a homeless woman who pleads for help on the street but is ignored by a passer-by. The song contrasts her suffering with the comfort of others, reminding listeners to reflect on their own humanity.

The theme of the song centers on compassion, responsibility, and the difference between the privileged and the marginalized. The song is composed of three stanzas with a recurring chorus. It also uses rhyming pairs like street–feet, denies–cries, twice–paradise, etc., to create a smooth lyrical flow. Visual images (e.g., “blisters on the soles of her feet”) and auditory images (e.g., “she calls out to the man on the street”) make the scene vivid. Devices such as anaphora (e.g., “you can… you can,” “Oh Lord… Oh Lord”), repetition (“think twice”), and irony in the use of the word ‘paradise’ intensify the message of the song. The song blends simple structure with powerful imagery and poetic devices to deliver a moving moral appeal against apathy. AN UNFORGETTABLE DAY My friend, yesterday was an unforgettable day for me. When we received a message from our son three days before, we were literally shocked. To see him off, we were going to Sulmona by the local train. The passengers in the train made room for my wife who was extremely sad. Everyone in the compartment noticed us. Then I thought I would explain the situation of us and the reason for my wife’s sadness. When I said that our only son was leaving to volunteer for war, a passenger said that we should thank God because his son had been sent to war the first day itself. Another passenger said that he had two sons and three nephews at the front. There was a debate about parental love. One said that it was not like bread which can be broken into pieces and split amongst the children in equal shares. Then a stout red faced man with blood shot eyes questioned if we gave life to our children for our own benefit.
We stared at him in distress. The one who had his son at the front since the first day of the war sighed and asked if

there was any one of us who wouldn’t gladly take his son’s place at the front if he could. He opined that if country was a natural necessity like bread, somebody must go to defend it. He added that when our sons die, they die happy and so, they didn’t want our tears. He also shared an experience of receiving a message from his son before dying. He said that he was dying satisfied at having ended his life in the best way he could have wished. That was why he was not mourning. Immediately my wife turned to him and asked if his son was really dead. We stared at her. And we could see the old man struggling for words to reply. We saw his face contracted and became horribly distorted. Then to our amazement, he broke into tears, and cried bitterly. We were deeply touched his his unexpected bursting out and all of us were sad too.

UNIT 4 WOODLAND WHISPERS 1. Shakuntalam : At a glance Kalidasa’s play Shakuntalam beautifully portrays the way our ancestors lived in close harmony with nature. It reminds us that breaking this bond with nature leads to destruction, while peaceful coexistence ensures balance and well-being. In Shakuntalam, Kalidasa shows that humans can live in harmony with nature through love, care, and respect. The hermitage is a peaceful place where plants and animals are treated like family members. The play teaches that when humans protect nature, nature, in turn, supports and nurtures human life.

The play opens with King Dushyanta pursuing a deer in the forest in his chariot. As he admires the grace and beauty of the animal, he prepares to shoot it. At that moment, a voice cautions him against killing the deer. Two hermits soon appear and explain that the deer belongs to their hermitage and is under their protection. They gently remind the king that weapons are meant to defend the innocent, not to harm the helpless. Respecting their wisdom, the king lowers his bow and returns the arrow to his quiver. Pleased with his conduct, the hermits bless him and invite him to visit Sage Kanva’s hermitage, where his foster daughter Shakuntala looks after the place in his absence.

When Dushyanta arrives at the hermitage, he is deeply impressed by the calm and sacred atmosphere. He observes parrots dropping grains of rice, oil-stained pounding stones lying around, and gentle deer roaming freely without fear. Realising the serenity of the place, the king waits silently so as not to disturb its peace. Soon, he notices Shakuntala along with her friends, Anasuya and Priyamvada, watering the plants. They care for the trees lovingly, treating them like members of their own family. They compare Shakuntala to a delicate jasmine creeper and delight in the natural beauty around them. The king is instantly captivated by Shakuntala’s grace, purity, and simplicity.

As Shakuntala bends down to water a creeper, a bee begins to hover around her, frightening her. Her friends teasingly suggest that she call upon King Dushyanta, the guardian of the hermitage, to protect her from the bee. The hermitage is shown as a place where human life, plants, and animals exist in perfect harmony, and nature is treated with love and reverence. Through this, the play suggests that human happiness and moral living are closely linked to respect for the natural world. SMILE ENGLISH 3

2. Trills and Thrills : Birdwatching in India : At a glance This lesson is an extract from Salim Ali’s book “Fall of a Sparrow”. Salim Ali is popularly known as the ‘Birdman of India’ and he was the first Indian to conduct a systematic bird survey across India. The lesson is about his few memorable experiences that he had during bird watching. Ornithology or the scientific study of birds was both a hobby and a profession for Salim Ali. It was full of adventure, rewards, punishment and disappointment. It was also the most peaceful of hobbies he ever knew. He recounts his personal experiences which were exciting and dangerous at the same time. He also understood that there were many things about birds which were not mentioned in books. He also concludes by saying that bird watching for more than fifty years gave him lot of pleasure and happiness. Meeting Baron Omar Rolf

Salim Ali recalls that field study of birds may be a peaceful task, it had its own dangers. In South India wild elephants can suddenly come at very close quarters and it can be terrifying. Among the elephants, a rogue or a female with a calf are more dangerous. During his visit to the Parambikulam, he came across a large group of Kadar adivasis and in their midst was a European male in khaki shorts. He was Baron Omar Rolf, an Austrian anthropologist. William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet, dramatist, and one of the central figures of 20th-century literature. Yeats’s writing style is distinguished by musical language, symbolic imagery, and a fusion of the mystical with the real. His poem “The Wild Swans at Coole” is a gentle, reflective piece in which the poet observes a group of swans on an autumn evening. The calm, beautiful setting makes him think deeply about change, ageing, and the passage of time. The main theme of the poem is the contrast between the poet’s ageing and the unchanging, youthful energy of the swans. While Yeats feels the effects of time on his own life—tiredness, loneliness, and the awareness that things have changed—the swans remain graceful, full of life, and constant in their companionship. The poem expresses a quiet sadness as well as admiration for the swans’ beauty and freedom. It reminds us that nature can remain eternal even as human life changes.

The poem opens with a picturesque description of the trees in their autumn beauty, the dry woodlands and the lake water mirroring the sky. The swans, those ‘brilliant creatures’ ‘mysterious and beautiful,’ paddling in the cold companionable streams or climbing the air are very much a part of nature. The depiction of the scenic beauty of the park and the graceful elegance of the swans inspire readers to value nature. The swans seem to represent lasting youth and beauty. They do not appear to be affected by the passage of time. They are not seen to yield to the onset of old- age. Instead, they ‘paddle’ in the ‘streams’, ‘unwearied’, ‘lover by lover’. As the poet notes,‘Their hearts have not grown old.’ The swans, unlike us, are majestic. They drift on the still water, climb the air, painting the sky with the bell beat of their wings and fly away before the poet realises they are gone. The poem is rich in images of youth and old- age.

The trees in their autumn beauty, the dry woodland paths and the twilight represent old- age. In contrast, the still sky could represent the seemingly-eternal youthful glory of the swans. They do not seem to grow old. They move about unwearied, lover by lover, paddling along the streams. The poet believes that this is because ‘their hearts have not grown old.’ ‘The bell-beat of the wings’, ‘trod with lighter tread’, ‘they paddle in the field’, ‘companionable streams or climb the air’ etc are some of the examples of alliteration. ‘And scatter wheeling in great broken rings’ is an example of assonance. Also the use of rhetorical question ‘To find they have flown away’ adds to the beauty of the poem.

The unchanging swans stand in symbolic contrast to Yeat’s sense of decline, while the political turbulence following the Easter Rising subtly echoes the poem’s atmosphere of uncertainty. Together, these elements reveal the poem as a meditation not only on nature’s beauty but on the fragility of life, love, and the passage of time.

UNIT 5 SONGS OF THE SELF 1. BELOVED BOLES: At a glance Beloved Boles by Maxim Gorky is a touching story that tells us about a narration from his friend. He was a student at Moscow who lived alongside the room of a Polish woman named Teresa. She was tall, strong, rough- looking, and had a loud, deep voice. He assumes she is unworthy of respect. Teresa is living a lonely, miserable life.Though she is rude and rough, she is tender, emotional, and loving. She wants the student to write a letter to Boles, her lover. He writes the letter as dictated by her. But soon she demands him to write another letter from Boles to Teresa. Then the student gets angry and tells her not to fool him any more. At last, the student feels empathy for her when he realizes that she has invented Boles because she has no one in the world to love her or to care for her.

He feels sorry and ashamed for misunderstanding her loneliness and recognizes the deep human need for affection. 2. PREFERENCE NATIONALE : At a glance The story Preference Nationale by Fatou Diome tells how difficult it is to prove our identity when the society doesn't accept us. The story is about a woman from Africa who is living in France. Even though she is educated and has a degree, she faces unfair treatment because of her colour and nationality. When she tries to get a job at a bakery, the owner refuses to give her the job as she is black and not French. Though she speak French, she fails to speak the dialect he mentions and thus gets rejected. Later, she applies for another job to teach the child of a French lady, but she also rejects her, saying she wants a European type person. The African lady feels hurt and angry because she is qualified and capable, but people only see her colour.

The story shows how immigrants and blacks are often treated badly and not given equal chance even when they deserve. It also teaches us that everyone should be treated fairly regardless of their colour and nationality. 3. MIRROR : At a glance The poem Mirror by Sylvia Plath deals with the themes of truth, identity, and ageing. The mirror speaks in the first person and claims that it has “no preconceptions” and reflects whatever it sees “just as it is.” Through this honest voice, the poet shows how human beings struggle to accept reality, especially the loss of youth and the passage of time.

The poem is rich in imagery. The mirror describes itself as “silver and exact,” creating a clear visual image of brightness and precision. The comparison of the mirror to “the eye of a little god, four- cornered” suggests an all-seeing, impartial power. Later, the mirror becomes a “lake,” an image that conveys depth and self-searching. The striking image of the old woman rising “like a terrible fish” vividly expresses the woman’s fear and shock at seeing her ageing self. Several poetic devices are effectively used. Personification is the most prominent device, as the mirror speaks, meditates, and reflects faithfully. Metaphor is used when the mirror is compared to a god and a lake, symbolising truth and self-examination. Simile appears in the line “like a terrible fish,” intensifying the horror of ageing. Symbolism is also important: the mirror symbolises truth, while candles and the moon symbolise illusion and false comfort.

In brief, the poem presents a woman who depends on the mirror to understand her identity. As she repeatedly confronts her reflection, she realises that her youthful self has disappeared and old age is inevitable. The poem powerfully conveys the conflict between harsh truth and comforting illusion, making it a deeply reflective and disturbing poem about human existence.

The Old Man with Enormous Wings by Gabriel Garcia Marquez About the Story: One gloomy afternoon, Pelayo discovers a frail old man with enormous wings lying face down in the mud. Frightened, he and his wife Elisenda inspect the man closely. Dressed in rags and barely able to speak in an unknown language, the old man appears more like a drenched grandfather than a divine being. They assume he’s a shipwrecked foreigner, but a neighbour insists he is an angel who has come for their sick child. The next day, the entire town crowds their courtyard, treating the angel like a spectacle. Pelayo locks him in the chicken coop (birds of a feather!), and when the child recovers, the couple briefly consider setting the angel free. Instead, Elisenda capitalizes on the situation, charging an admission fee to see the angel. Pilgrims and others from afar visit the angel, hoping for miracles.

The angel, passive and enduring, does not resist the indignities he suffers—being pelted with food, poked by cripples, and jeered at like a circus animal. Despite his wings, his only strength seems to be his infinite patience. The people soon lose interest when a new attraction—a spider-woman with a tragic tale—arrives. Still, the couple become wealthy, build a mansion, and improve their lives, ignoring the fact that the angel’s condition has worsened. As time passes; the angel becomes weaker, grows almost blind, and remains bedraggled, but he survives. One day, as Elisenda cuts onions in the kitchen, she sees the angel struggling to fly. At last, he lifts off clumsily and disappears into the distance. Elisenda watches until he becomes a mere dot on the horizon, relieved that the strange burden has finally left their lives.

In the Attic by Wladyslaw Szpilman About the Story: “In the Attic” is an excerpt from Wladyslaw Szpilman’s survivor testimony tiled “ The Pianist”. It revolves around the unusual friendship between Szpilman and Captain Wilm Hosenfeld, a German officer. Hosenfeld discovers Szpilman hiding in an abandoned building and asks him to play the piano. Amidst the unrest and the precarious circumstances that prevailed, Szpilman plays Chopin’s Nocturne in C- sharp minor, which moves Hosenfeld deeply. The officer offers to take Szpilman to a safer location and it is then that he learns that Szpilman was a Jew. Instead of turning him in, he offers to help Szpilman and advices him to stay in a loft which was a safer place than the loft where he had originally hid. Hosenfeld promises to bring Szpilman food. At this point Szpilman realises that he is being helped by a German officer.

Hosenfeld admits to the fact that he is ashamed of identifying himself as a German and feels a sense of horror and shame at what has been happening. Despite being on opposite sides of the conflict, Szpilman and Hosenfeld find common ground through music. After three days Hosenfeld returns with several loaves of bread and jam which would eventually keep Szpilman alive for days to come. He tells Szpilman that the war would soon be over and that he must ‘hang on’. The gesture instills in him confidence and a renewed hope for survival. Szpilman continues to live in isolation often without human contact for long intervals of time with the only sound he hears is artillery fire and of soldiers going up and down the stairs where he was hiding. He also endures extreme cold, lack of sanitation and pitiable living conditions amidst living in constant fear of discovery, arrest and deportation to concentration camps.

The officer returns one last time on December 12 and brings along with him a larger supply of bread and a warm eiderdown. He tells Szpilman that he would be leaving Warsaw and that he must under no circumstance lose heart. Hosenfeld reminds Szpilman that if they have survived the inferno for over five years, it was God’s will. At the parting moment, Szpilman expresses his gratitude and promises to repay Hosenfeld’s kindness and assistance that helped him survive the war. That was the last time he

saw the officer. Szpilman survives another year. The passage of time gnaws his conscience and he recounts the loss of his family, the traumatic experiences distress him. On the morning of January 15, Szpilman listens to announcements on the street of the defeat of Germany 28and the liberation of Warsaw. He stays in a delusional state not knowing what to do or how to react to the news. Then he comes across voices of women and children. He runs downstairs and peeps out to get a view of the street and finds a woman police officer and a lady carrying a bundle on her head. As Szpilman tries to talk to the lady, she shrieks in fear seeing him wearing a German coat and suspecting that he is a German. Szpilman was wearing the coat Captain Hosenfeld had given him which leads to the misunderstanding and him being reprimanded by Polish soldiers. Later, the soldiers understand the situation and Szpilman is rescued and finally walks free.

The friendship between Szpilman and Hosenfeld remains a powerful testament to the human capacity for connection and compassion, even in the most challenging circumstances. Szpilman’s story is a testament to the human spirit’s ability to persevere in the face of adversity.

UNIT III - TRUMPETS OF CHANGE War by Luigi Pirandello About the Story: Luigi Pirandello’s short story War is set in the context of World War I. The action takes place on a train carrying a group of passengers, most of whom are parents of soldiers fighting at the front. Among them is a grieving couple whose only son has recently been called to war. The mother, devastated by this, remains silent and withdrawn, while the father, though sorrowful, attempts to stay calm and

composed. As the train moves, the passengers engage in a conversation about their children and cost of war. The discussion soon turns into a debate about patriotic duty. One father, whose son has died in battle, argues that parents should not mourn selfishly. He claims that once children grow up, they belong to the country, not to their families. He insists that soldiers go to war for honour, and parents should take pride in the sacrifice rather than grieve the loss. His words seem to carry conviction, and for the moment, the other passengers appear to accept his reasoning. The grieving father whose son had recently been conscripted listens carefully to the discussion but does not speak at first. The other passengers try to comfort themselves by holding on to the idea that their sons are destined to die for a noble cause.

They convince themselves that the children are fulfilling their patriotic duty and that as parents they should be proud rather than sad. This notion provides some relief, and they try to suppress their sorrow.

However, as the conversation progresses, the man who had at first spoken so confidently about the nobility of sacrifice begins to show signs of grief and pain. His voice starts to tremble, and his expressions betray the enormity of his sorrow.This transformation is triggered by the grieving mother who had been silent. At one point, she breaks in with the question to the man if his son is truly dead. The man is unable to respond at first. Then, overwhelmed by emotion, he breaks down, realizing at that very moment the depth of his suffering and the extent of his self-deception.

This transforms the atmosphere in the compartment. The passengers, who had been trying to rationalize their pain now recognize the undeniable grief in their own hearts and souls. They had tried to convince themselves that the sacrifices of their sons were necessary and honourable, but now they see they cannot escape the unbearable weight of inevitable loss. Even the strongest conviction of patriotic duty cannot negate the sorrow of losing one’s child. In this story, Pirandello shows us little we know ourselves. People often successfully hide their pain even from themselves behind a dark curtain of high- sounding ideals. The curtain will, however, sooner or later, be ripped away from our own eyes at least. The story highlights the universal anguish of parents who send their children to war. It is a powerful reflection on the cost of ‘duty’ and the explosion of suppressed suffering.

A Piece of String by Guy de Maupassant About the Story:

Guy de Maupassant’s short story A Piece of String is set in a small French village and revolves around Hauchecome, an innocent peasant, whose life is turned upside down by a simple misunderstanding. The story begins on a market day in Goderville, when the villagers gather to trade goods and share news. Hauchecome, a humble and thrifty farmer, stoops to pick up a small piece of string on the ground, as he believes that anything useful should be saved. Unfortunately, this action is

witnessed by Malandain, an old enemy, who misinterprets it and spreads the rumour that Hauchecome had picked up something precious. When news spreads that a pocketbook containing money has gone missing, suspicion immediately falls on Hauchecome. He is summoned to the Mayor’s office, where the Mayor, a pompous personality, questions him sternly. Hauchecome tries to explain that he had only picked up a piece of string, showing it to the Mayor in an attempt to establish his innocence. However, the Mayor does not believe him, insisting that Malandain, a reputable man, had seen him pick up the pocketbook. Hauchecome is allowed to go, but the seed of doubt has been planted in the minds of the villagers The villagers crowd around Hauchecome, demanding an explanation and making fun of his protestations of innocence. The man tirelessly retells the story of the piece of string to anyone who will listen, hoping to clear his name.

Even when the pocketbook is found and returned by someone else, the villagers continue to suspect Hauchecome of being involved in the ‘fraud.’ They laugh at his explanations, dismissing these as lies or excuses. Hauchecome becomes obsessed with defending his honour and clearing his name. Each time he tells the story, he is met with scorn and disbelief. Through repeated accusations and ridicule, the villagers drive Hauchecome to despair. The weight of suspicion breaks him down. Finally, he falls ill and dies, haunted by the injustice of his experience. In his final delirious moments, he still mumbles the tale of the piece of string, and dies a victim of gossip, misunderstanding and prejudice.

UNIT V - SONGS OF THE SELF Beloved Boles by Maxim Gorky About the Story

Beloved Boles by Maxim Gorky is a touching story about loneliness, imagination, and the deep human need for affection. The story is narrated by a young student living in Moscow, whose room faces that of a Polish woman named Teresa. At first, the student is uncomfortable around her. Teresa is tall, strong, and rough- looking, with a loud bass voice, bushy eyebrows, and a coarse face. She often appears drunk, with messy hair and bleary eyes, and her loud greetings make him uneasy. Because of her strange and intimidating appearance, he always keeps his door shut when she is at home. One day, Teresa approaches the student with an unusual request. She asks him to write a letter to a man named Boleslav Kashput, whom she lovingly calls “Boles,” her “beloved,” her “heart of gold.” Though surprised by her tender words, the student writes the letter as she dictates.

When she returns later asking him to write a reply “from Boles,” he grows suspicious. Her nervousness and trembling hands confuse him further. Finally, irritated, he accuses her of lying and trying to fool him. Hurt and frightened, Teresa runs away in distress. Feeling uneasy after their encounter, the student visits her room and discovers the truth. Teresa breaks down and confesses that Boles does not exist at all. She has invented him because she has no one in the world who shows her affection or speaks to her kindly. The letters allow her to imagine that someone loves her and cares for her. Writing to Boles and receiving replies makes her feel less lonely and gives her the illusion of being valued. When others read the letters

aloud, she feels, for a moment, that Boles is truly by her side. Hearing her painful confession, the student is overwhelmed with sympathy and shame for misunderstanding her. From that day onwards, the student begins writing letters to Boles and replies to Teresa regularly, twice a week. She listens to them and weeps loudly, moved by the imaginary affection she longs for so deeply. In return, she mends his torn clothes and looks after his small needs. Her simple acts of care show her gratitude for the emotional comfort the letters provide. After some months, Teresa is arrested for unknown reasons, and the narrator believes she must be dead now. Reflecting on her life, he realises how people like Teresa, who have suffered bitterness and loneliness, hunger more than anyone for kindness and tenderness.

The story ends with a powerful message: while society judges people from the outside, it often fails to see their emotional pain, and the lack of love can drive people to create their own fragile fantasies to survive.

Préférence Nationale by Fatou Diome About the Story:

Fatou Diome’s Préférence Nationale is a powerful and deeply personal narrative that exposes the everyday racism, prejudice, and structural discrimination faced by immigrants in France. The narrator, a Senegalese woman living in Strasbourg, describes how the French system creates barriers for foreigners, especially through laws that quietly delay or deny citizenship. She sarcastically remarks that even her Senegalese cat has official papers, while she, a human being, is denied recognition. Her sharp humour highlights how laws, though created by governments, are enforced and strengthened by ordinary people who apply them rigidly in daily life. In her search for work, the narrator responds to a newspaper advertisement from a city-center bakery seeking a salesgirl. Despite her qualifications, her French friend discourages her, failing to understand the challenges immigrants face.

Determined to survive, the narrator visits the bakery, only to encounter racial prejudice face to face. The bakery owner, a man with a German moustache and a hat in French colours, dismisses her the moment he sees her skin. He insists she speak the local Alsatian dialect, knowing she cannot, and finally humiliates her by suggesting she should “work in her own country.” His refusal reveals how préférence nationale, the idea of privileging French natives over foreigners, operates not just in law but in people’s attitudes. Still unemployed, the narrator later applies for another job as a French tutor. When she meets the woman, a supermarket cashier, she is once again rejected purely because she is not ‘European-type.’ Despite having a degree and more competence than the woman judging her, she is dismissed due to her race.

The narrator responds with dignity and sharp wit, exposing the hypocrisy of someone who looks down on her while lacking the education she possesses. The woman’s final racist insult only reinforces the cruelty the narrator faces, but she remains emotionally strong, remarking that unlike those who turn red with anger or shame, her skin “always keeps its dignity.” Through these incidents, Diome portrays the harsh realities of immigrants who struggle not because of a lack of qualifications, but because of systemic racism and social prejudice. Despite this, the narrator’s voice remains strong, intelligent, and courageous as she challenges injustice with satire, truth, and a refusal to lose her self-respect. Ultimately, the story reveals that identity is not granted by society’s approval but shaped by one’s inner strength, dignity, and resilience. 1. In recent years, community libraries have begun to reappear in towns and villages, taking on new forms and purposes. Unlike traditional libraries that focused mainly on silent reading, modern community libraries function as shared learning spaces. They offer books, newspapers, digital resources, and even workshops for people of all ages. These libraries play a crucial role in promoting reading habits, especially among children who may not have access to books at home. Community libraries also help bridge the digital divide. Many of them provide free internet access and basic computer training, enabling people to apply for jobs, access government services, and learn new skills. For elderly people, these spaces offer a sense of belonging, while young learners benefit from group activities such as storytelling sessions and reading clubs. Beyond education, community libraries strengthen social bonds.

They encourage interaction among people from different backgrounds and promote values such as cooperation and mutual respect. In a world increasingly dominated by individual screen time, these libraries remind us of the importance of shared spaces for collective growth. DISCOURSES CHARACTER SKETCH King Dushyanta “King Dushyanta’s character is a blend of a fierce warrior and a humble protector." Based on the opening scenes of the play, King Dushyanta is portrayed as a multifaceted character who embodies the qualities of a heroic leader, a skilled hunter, and a respectful follower of Dharma (righteous duty). Initially, he is seen as a man of action and vigor, pursuing a deer with intense focus and expert skill. His poetic descriptions of the fleeing animal reveal a refined, aesthetic side; he is not merely a predator but a connoisseur of beauty, capable of admiring the "bending neck" and "graceful leaps" of his prey even as he prepares to strike. However, the most defining trait of his character in this part of the play is his humility and sense of duty.

Despite holding supreme power, he immediately halts his pursuit at the command of a simple hermit. By "bowing low" and restoring his arrow to the quiver, Dushyanta demonstrates that his ego is subordinate to sacred law. He transitions seamlessly from a fierce warrior to a "shining example of kings," proving that his true strength lies in his self-restraint and his commitment to protecting the innocent rather than merely asserting his dominance over nature.
REVIEW "The opening of the play moves from a scene of 'aggression' to a scene of 'grace.' Prepare a review highlighting how the playwright achieves this transition through the King's actions."

Review: The Hunt and the Hermitage (Act I) The play opens with high-octane energy. The vivid description of the deer’s flight creates a sense of breathless speed, instantly pulling the audience into the King's world of the hunt. The transition from the dusty, adrenaline-filled chase to the quiet, disciplined boundaries of the hermitage is masterfully handled, shifting the tone from aggression to grace. King Dushyanta is introduced not as a one-dimensional ruler, but as a man of high sensitivity. His ability to describe the deer’s "half-chewed grass" and "bending neck" shows a deep connection to nature, even while he pursues it. This makes his later submission to the Hermit feel natural rather than forced. The Hermit, though physically powerless compared to the King, wields a moral authority that defines the play’s ethical compass.

The core of this section is the lesson on the true purpose of power. The Hermit’s plea—that weapons are meant to protect the broken-hearted, not strike the innocent— serves as a powerful reminder of Dharma (righteousness). The King’s decision to put his arrow back in the quiver is the first major "victory" of the play, though it is a victory of character rather than a victory of the hunt. This opening is a brilliant study in restraint. It establishes Dushyanta as a hero worthy of our respect, not because of his skill with a bow, but because of his willingness to listen to his conscience. It sets a beautiful stage for the romantic and spiritual journey that follows.

An introduction to Shākuntalam As part of a student exchange programme, you engage in a session on theatre with a group of Class 10 learners from your neighbouring state. Prepare an introduction to Shākuntalam for their benefit. You may highlight the theatrical techniques, the setting, characters and sequence of events. Introduction to Shākuntalam: A Journey from Court to Forest Good morning, everyone! Today, we are stepping back nearly 1,500 years into the world of Kalidasa, often called the "Shakespeare of India." His most famous play, Abhijnanashakuntalam, is not just a story; it is a sensory experience of ancient India.

1. The Setting: Two Different Worlds The play moves between two contrasting locations: • The Royal Court: Representing power, structure, and social duty. • The Hermitage (Ashram): A sacred forest sanctuary where humans, animals, and plants live in harmony. This is a place of peace where even a King must set aside his weapons. 2. The Main Characters • King Dushyanta: A noble and powerful ruler, but also a man of deep poetic feeling and humility. • Shakuntala: The daughter of a sage and a celestial nymph. She represents the purity of nature itself. • The Forest Dwellers: Including the hermits and Shakuntala’s friends, who act as the moral conscience of the story.

3. The Sequence of Events (The Opening) The play begins with a high-speed chase. King Dushyanta enters in a chariot, pursuing a deer. Just as he is about to shoot, he is stopped by a voice from a hermitage. This moment is the "inciting incident"—it changes the King from a hunter into a guest of the forest, leading him to meet Shakuntala. 4. Unique Theatrical Techniques Sanskrit theatre uses specific techniques that you might find different from modern movies: • Nandimukha (The Prologue): The play begins with a prayer to Lord Shiva to bless the performance. • The Sutradhara: A "Stage Manager" or narrator who introduces the play to the audience. • Rasa (Emotion): The goal of the play is to make the audience feel a specific emotion. In this act, we move from Vira Rasa (Heroic/Energy) during the hunt to Shanta Rasa (Peace) at the hermitage.

DISCOURSES DIARY In the lesson "Trills and Thrills," Dr. Salim Ali describes a heart-pounding encounter with a wild tusker while birdwatching in the jungles of Parambikulam, while is accompanied by Baron Omar Rolf, who runs away without even seeing the elephant. Prepare the diary for Dr. Salim Ali February 17, 1946 Tuesday What a heart-stopping day! It began peacefully enough. I set out early with Baron Omar Rolf and a forest guard, trekking through tall grass to find the Broad-tailed Grass Warbler. The air was still, and the grass was so high it swallowed us up. Then, everything changed in a heartbeat. As we rounded a bend, the guard suddenly ducked. My heart nearly stopped—a massive tusker was walking right toward us! I didn't wait a second; I turned and ran as fast as my legs could carry me, shouting for Omar to do the same. I have never seen anyone move so fast!

The Baron sprinted past me like a professional athlete, his long legs flying. When I finally caught up to him—hot, breathless, and shaking—he looked at me and whispered, "What was it?" He hadn't even seen the elephant! He just saw me running and took off. Looking back, it’s quite funny. The poor elephant probably didn't even notice us; he just wandered off into the brush. But it was a sharp reminder: birdwatching may be a "peaceful" hobby, but in the wild, you must always be ready to move NARRATIVE During his birdwatching travels in 1946, Dr. Salim Ali along with his friend Baron Omar Rolf had a thrilling and funny encounter with a wild elephant at Parambikulam. Prepare a likely narrative

In February 1946, I was exploring the beautiful jungles of Parambikulam. My goal was to study the nesting habits of the Broad-tailed Grass Warbler. I was not alone; I was joined by an Austrian anthropologist named Baron Omar Rolf, who was very keen on birdwatching. Guided by a forest guard, we were walking along a narrow animal trail. The grass was very thick and stood over five feet high. Suddenly, as we turned a bend, the guard ducked down in excitement and pointed ahead. My heart skipped a beat—a massive wild tusker was striding down the same path, coming directly toward us! Knowing how dangerous a wild elephant can be at close range, I didn't waste a second. I turned and fled as fast as I could, motioning to the Baron to do the same. I have never seen anyone react so quickly! The Baron spun around with the agility of a cat and sprinted away on his long legs. He was so fast that he outdistanced me by a hundred yards in no time.

I finally caught up to him, hot and panting. The Baron looked at me and whispered breathlessly, "What was it?" I couldn't help but be amused. He had been running for his life without even seeing the elephant! As it turned out, the poor tusker had likely never noticed us and simply veered away into the grass. This incident is a constant reminder to me that while birdwatching is a peaceful pursuit, it is never lacking in thrills. As the famous "Birdman of India," Dr. Salim Ali, once said, birdwatching is not just a hobby; it is an adventure that helps us feel connected to the world. But birds are more than just pretty to look at.

They are like "nature's messengers." When birds start to disappear from an area, it is a warning sign that the environment is in trouble— perhaps because of pollution, or because too many trees are being cut down. By watching birds, we learn to notice these changes before it is too late.

The good news is that we can help! You don’t need to do anything big to make a difference. You can: Plant a tree in your garden. Keep a bowl of clean water for birds during the hot summer. APPRECIATION THE WILD SWANS AT COOLE -W. B YEATS W.B. Yeats, one of the most celebrated poets of the 20th century, is renowned for his lyrical poetry that intricately weaves themes of nature, love, and the complexities of human emotions. His work often captures a delicate balance of beauty and melancholy, inviting the reader to ponder profound philosophical thoughts. “The Wild Swans at Coole” stands out as a significant piece, embodying Yeats’ deep admiration for the natural world while reflecting on the relentless passage of time and the inevitable transformations that accompany it. Through this poem, Yeats expresses a poignant exploration of ageing and the bittersweet nature of life's

fleeting moments alongside the enduring beauty of the world around us. In the poem, Yeats describes visiting Coole Park, where he sees a group of sixty wild swans swimming gracefully on the lake. He marvels at their majesty, freedom, and eternal beauty, which contrasts with his own ageing and mortality. The poet notices that although the swans remain unchanged, he himself feels the effects of time, realising that life is fleeting and full of change. He compares the swans’ lively, eternal nature with the temporary joys and sorrows of human life. The poem ends with a melancholic reflection that life is transient, yet the beauty of nature remains a source of inspiration and comfort. Yeats skillfully employs a variety of poetic devices to enhance the richness of the poem.

Vivid imagery brings the scene to life, allowing readers to visualise the swans with lines such as “their hearts have not grown old” and “their heads are bent gracefully,” fostering an emotional connection with their timeless beauty. Symbolism plays a crucial role, with the swans representing not just eternal grace but also the passage of time—a reminder of life’s impermanence. The use of alliteration and assonance contributes to the poem's musicality, creating a lyrical flow that immerses readers in the enchantment of the natural world. Additionally, the contrast between the changing life and the unchanging beauty of nature makes the poem more thoughtful. In my opinion, I find “The Wild Swans at Coole” a thought-provoking work. It invites us to not only appreciate the wonder of nature but also to confront our own lives and the transient nature of our experiences. Yeats uses simple but very meaningful language.

This makes the poem easy to understand and also touches our feelings. The poem shows the lasting beauty of nature and the short life of human beings. It reminds us to enjoy nature and value every moment of our lives.

Moscow, October 18, 1888 Dear Ivan, I hope this letter finds you well in St. Petersburg. My studies here are progressing, but tonight my mind is far from my textbooks. I am sitting in my small room, looking at a pair of mended socks on my desk, and feeling a weight of shame that I cannot easily describe. For months, I lived next to a woman named Teresa. To be honest, Ivan, I treated her with nothing but "horror" and disgust. She had a coarse face and a deep, masculine bass voice that repulsed me. Because I am a "Student," I looked down on her as a sub-human creature—someone far beneath my intellect and social standing.

One day, she asked me to write a letter to her lover, Boles. I mocked her, thinking her stories were a "pack of lies." But then, I discovered the tragic truth: Boles did not exist. This lonely woman had invented a lover just to feel a spark of affection in a world that treated her with total indifference. I realized then that I was the "blockhead," not her. My education had made me clever, but it had also made me heartless. I began writing her letters twice a week, and in return, she mended my clothes with a quiet, motherly care. We found a strange, beautiful friendship in that small gap between our rooms. Teresa was taken to prison recently "for some reason or the other," and I fear she may never return. She has vanished, forgotten by everyone but me. She taught me that behind the coarsest exterior lies a "human creature" starving for kindness.

I have learned that the greatest tragedy is not being poor, but being invisible to those who live "not three yards away." Write back when you can. I find the silence of the hallway much louder now that she is gone. Yours lovingly, Mr. Student

MIRROR- SYLVIA PLATH Mirror is a confessional poem by Sylvia Plath, a famous American modern poet known for her confessional poems. This poem is a lyric that explores themes of truth, time, ageing, and identity. The poem is spoken in the voice of a mirror, which honestly reflects whatever it sees. Through the mirror, the poet shows how human beings find it difficult to accept the truth about themselves In the beginning, the mirror describes itself as “silver and exact,” showing that it reflects everything truthfully without judgment. It has no feelings, like love or dislike, and is introduced as “The eye of a little god, four-cornered” which sees everything clearly and truthfully, like God who misses nothing, with the rectangular shape of the mirror. It judges no one but observes everything. Most of the time, it reflects a pink wall and feels connected to it.

When people stand in front of the mirror or when darkness falls, their faces and the darkness repeatedly replace the wall reflected in the mirror. In the second part of the poem, the mirror becomes a lake, suggesting depth. We can see a woman bends over it and searches for her true self. The mirror shows her real appearance, which makes her unhappy so She turns to candlelight and moonlight because they hide reality. Even though she turns away, the mirror faithfully reflects her as she is, People love false reflections that make them feel better, even if they are not their true self. Every morning, she sees herself growing old. The poem ends with the image of an old woman rising in the mirror, showing the loss of youth and the fear of ageing. The poem is rich in poetic devices.

Personification is used when the mirror speaks, as in “I have no preconceptions.” Metaphor is seen in “The Eye of a little god” and “Now I am a Lake.” Imagery is used in “It is pink, with speckles.” Simile appears in “like a terrible fish,” highlighting the fear of old age. Symbolism is evident as the mirror stands for truth, and “the candles or the moon” represent illusion. These devices add depth and meaning to the poem. In conclusion, Mirror is a powerful poem that shows how people find it difficult to accept reality. Through simple language and strong images, Sylvia Plath presents the painful truth about ageing and self-identity. The poem prompts us to think deeply about truth and self-acceptance, making it memorable and meaningful.

A very Old Man with Enormous Wings by Gabriel García Márquez is a powerful and symbolic story that explores human behaviour, compassion, cruelty, and the way society treats those who are different. Through the character of the old man with wings, the author presents a deep criticism of human selfishness and lack of empathy. The story begins when Pelayo and Elisenda find an old man lying helplessly in their courtyard. His enormous wings make him appear strange and mysterious, yet his weak and miserable condition makes him look more human than divine. Instead of treating him with kindness and care, the couple and the villagers see him as an object of curiosity. This shows how people are often more interested in the unusual than in the suffering of others.

At first, there is confusion about whether the old man is an angel. Some expect miracles from him. When their expectations are not fulfilled, their interest slowly fades. Pelayo and Elisenda exploit the situation by fencing their yard and charging money from visitors. The angel is treated like a circus animal, and people throw stones at him, pull his feathers, and disturb him constantly. This reflects how society often uses the weak and the helpless for personal benefit instead of protecting them. The angel’s character stands in sharp contrast to the cruelty of humans. His greatest supernatural quality is patience. He silently tolerates all kinds of suffering without anger or revenge. His
endurance makes him a symbol of quiet dignity and forgiveness. Through him, Márquez shows that true greatness lies in tolerance and compassion rather than power or authority.

The story also criticizes blind faith and shallow beliefs. People are quick to believe in miracles but lose interest when the angel does not satisfy their expectations. The arrival of the spider woman proves that people prefer simple and entertaining stories to deep and meaningful truths. This highlights the superficial nature of human curiosity. The ending of the story is highly symbolic. When the angel finally regains strength and flies away, Elisenda feels relieved, not because he is free, but because he is no longer a burden to her life. This shows her selfish attitude and lack of emotional connection. The angel’s flight represents freedom from suffering and the triumph of patience over cruelty. In conclusion, the lesson teaches that kindness and empathy are essential qualities in life. It warns us against judging others based on appearance and exploiting those who are weak.
The story encourages us to develop compassion and humanity, reminding us that even small act of kindness can bring hope and light into the lives of others.

The angel is the most striking and symbolic character in the story. Though he has enormous wings, he does not appear majestic or divine. Instead, he looks weak, old, and miserable. His physical appearance contrasts sharply with our traditional idea of an angel. He is dressed like a ragpicker, dirty and half-plucked, which makes people doubt his identity. The most important quality of the angel is his patience. Even when he is locked in a chicken coop, poked by curious visitors, and treated like a circus animal, he never protests or shows anger. People throw stones at him, pull his feathers, and disturb him constantly, yet he endures everything silently. His tolerance and calmness make him morally superior to the humans around him. The angel also symbolizes suffering and endurance. He becomes a victim of human cruelty, greed, and ignorance.

While the villagers exploit him for money and entertainment, he remains indifferent to fame or attention. His only concern seems to be survival. Though people see him as strange and useless, he shows a quiet dignity. His eventual recovery and flight suggest hope and freedom. His escape represents liberation from suffering and the triumph of patience over cruelty. Thus, the angel is not great because of his wings, but because of his endurance, humility, and forgiveness. He teaches us that true divinity lies in compassion, patience, and silent strength rather than in power or appearance.
