DISCOURSES I. “In the Attic” by Władysław Szpilman powerfully portrays the theme of human endurance and the will to survive amidst the horrors of war and persecution. It's a survival testemony that reflects the never ending resilience of human spirit. Prepare a detailed Review of ‘In the Attic’ focusing on its characterization, theme and plot development.

In the Attic is a touching survival story based on the real-life experiences of Władysław Szpilman, a Jewish pianist who struggles to stay alive during World War II. Set against the ruins of war-torn Warsaw, the narrative highlights the strength of the human spirit and the power of hope even in the darkest times. The central character, Szpilman, is portrayed as a quiet, sensitive, and deeply artistic man. At the beginning, he lives a normal life as a pianist, but war turns hisworld upside down. As he loses his family and freedom, his character develops into one of great courage and endurance. Though physically weak and starving, he never gives up the will to live.

Another important character is the German soldier who unexpectedly helps Szpilman. Though he belongs to the enemy side, he shows kindness and humanity by giving him food and protecting him. This soldier represents compassion even in cruel times and reminds us that goodness can exist anywhere. One of the major themes is survival and resilience. Szpilman’s struggle shows how humans can survive extreme hardship with hope and determination. Another theme is identity under threat. As a Jewish man and an artist, Szpilman’s very existence is in danger, yet he clings to his identity as a pianist.Music as a connection is also a powerful theme. Music becomes a symbol of life and hope. When Szpilman plays the piano for the soldier, it creates a deep emotional bond between them. The story also reflects compassion and humanity. The soldier’s unexpected kindness proves that even during war, people can rise above hatred.

Finally, freedom after war is shown when Szpilman survives to see the end of the war and regains his dignity and life. When Nazis invade Poland, Szpilman’s life slowly collapses. His family is taken away, and he is left alone to survive in hiding. He takes shelter in ruined buildings and in an attic, living in constant fear of being discovered. Hunger, loneliness, and illness weaken him, but he continues to fight for life. The turning point comes when he meets the German officer. Instead of arresting him, the soldier shows sympathy and secretly supports him. Szpilman plays the piano for the officer. This moment highlights the power of art and humanity. The story ends with the war coming to an end. Szpilman survives and returns to his profession as a pianist, symbolizing hope and freedom. In the Attic is a deeply moving story of courage, hope, and kindness.

It teaches us that even in times of extreme cruelty, humanity and compassion can still shine. The story reminds readers to value life, freedom, and empathy. Through Szpilman’s journey, we learn that hope and resilience can help us overcome even the darkest moments in history

2, The German officer shows empathy towards Szpilman choosing kindness instead of violence and brutality. Prepare the diary entry of the officer on the day of their last meeting before he leaves Warsaw

December 12, 1944 Tonight, silence presses against my ears more cruelly than gunfire ever did. I have just left that broken man behind in the attic — Władysław Szpilman, a Jew, a pianist, and perhaps the last living soul in this ruined city. I should have reported him. That is what a German officer is trained to do. That is what duty demanded of me. Yet my hands refused to move, my voice refused to betray him. When he sat at that ruined piano and played, the world I believed in collapsed. In those trembling notes, I heard humanity crying out beneath the boots of war. He was not my enemy. He was a starving artist clinging to life with dignity I no longer recognize in my own uniform. All my life I was taught that obedience is honour. But today I discovered that obedience can also be cowardice. I gave him food. I gave him a coat. I gave him hope. In doing so, I may have signed my own death warrant. The Red Army is close now.
My comrades are desperate. Our cause is crumbling. If they find out what I have done, I will be shot as a traitor.

And yet — for the first time in years — I feel calm and true. The war has stripped me of illusions, of faith in orders, of pride in my rank. It has turned men into wolves and cities into graves. But tonight, in a shattered building with a half-dead pianist, I reclaimed something the war tried to kill in me — my conscience. I am afraid. Afraid of capture. Afraid of execution. Afraid of what history will call men like me. But more than that, I am afraid of becoming a man who survives by crushing the innocent. If this war ends — and God, I pray it does — I hope Szpilman lives to play again. I hope the world remembers that even in the darkest ruins, a man can still choose mercy over murder. If I die, let it be known that on this night, I stopped being a soldier of hatred and became, once more, a human being. — Wilm Hosenfeld

Good morning to one and all. Today, I rise not merely to deliver a speech, but to give voice to a silent human tragedy — the tragedy of refugees. Every year on June 20, the world observes World Refugee Day. But for over 80 million displaced people worldwide, every day is a refugee day. Every sunrise greets them with uncertainty. Every sunset reminds them of what they have lost — their homes, their security, their loved ones, and often, their dignity. According to the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, nearly 26 million

people today live as refugees outside their countries of origin. These are not numbers on a page. These are mothers who carried their children across borders. These are fathers who stayed back to fight or were lost forever. These are children who have forgotten what a classroom looks like and have learned instead the language of fear. War does not only destroy buildings.It destroys childhoods, futures, and faith in humanity. Refugees flee because they must — because staying means death, persecution, hunger, or imprisonment. They leave behind graves of their ancestors, the walls that heard their laughter, and the streets that knew their footsteps. They carry their entire lives in a small bag and their memories in a broken heart. Refugees are forced to live in overcrowded camps, often without adequate food, clean water, shelter, or healthcare. Diseases spread easily. Trauma goes untreated.
Children grow up without education, without stability, and without hope. Many of them have never known a world without conflict. They are not running towards luxury. They are running away from death.

The global response to this crisis has been painfully unequal. While some countries shoulder the responsibility of hosting millions, others turn away, building walls instead of bridges. The distribution of humanitarian aid remains unjust, and political interests often take priority over human lives. This is why the refugee crisis is not only a political issue. It is a moral issue. It is a human issue. Dear friends, imagine this question for a moment: If war came to our city tonight, if bombs fell on our homes, if our schools were reduced to rubble — would we not also become refugees? The only difference between “us” and “them” is geography and fate. Refugees do not ask for charity. They ask for safety. They ask for dignity. They ask for a chance to rebuild their lives. On this World Refugee Day, let us move beyond sympathy to solidarity. Let us replace indifference with empathy. Let us choose compassion over convenience.
Let us work towards a world where no child has to grow up in a refugee camp, where no mother has to choose between hunger and bullets. Thank you. Let humanity guide us all.

PHRASAL VERBS A) fall on – attack suddenly or be the responsibility of. Eg: Then his glance fell on the door to the other room. B) stand by – support someone or be ready to act. Eg :We went into the next room where a piano stood by the wall. C) turn on – start a machine or device; also means to excite or suddenly attack. Eg: Through the paper, I felt several loaves and something soft, which later turned out to be jam wrapped in greaseproof paper. D) come in – enter a place. Eg : The guards saw me come in here, and I mustn’t stay long. The first hard frosts came in the middle of December. E) hang on – wait or hold tightly. Eg:” You must hang on, do you hear?” F) went over – examined or reviewed carefully (past tense of go over). Eg : In my mind, I went over every Christmas before and during the war. G) set up – arrange, organize, or establish.

Eg: Radio loudspeakers set up somewhere nearby were broadcasting announcements in Polish of the defeat of Germany and the liberation of Warsaw. H) put it on – wear something or pretend. Eg : I had already put it on when I suddenly heard the rhythmic footsteps of guards out in the road again. I) sink on – to gradually lean or collapse onto something. Eg : I sank on my mattress, utterly dejected, and lay there until something new came to my ears: J) take to one’s heels – run away quickly. Eg : She stared at me, dropped her bundle and took to her heels with a shriek of, “A German!” K) look out – be careful or watch for danger. Eg : Looking out of my little window a few minutes later, I saw that the whole building was surrounded. L) walk through – practice or explain step-by-step. Eg : After two weeks, well cared for by the military, I walked through the streets of Warsaw without fear, a free man, for the first time in almost six years.

M) look over – examine or check something quickly. Eg : I looked over to the north of the city, where the ghetto had been, where half a million Jews had been murdered— there was nothing left of it. N) go on – continue or happen. Eg : Tomorrow I must begin a new life, with nothing but death behind me. I went on my way. LANGUAGE ELEMENTS

Answers: SET 1 1. B) Within a darksome bed 2. It suggests that it is not the strength but the mindset that makes success. 3. This line represents self-determination. 4. When it took the decision to do its best. APPRECIATION THE SEEDLING -PAUL LAURENCE DUNBAR

Paul Laurence Dunbar stands out as a significant American poet renowned for his impactful poetry that often explores themes of hope, struggle, and resilience. His work reflects a profound insight into both life and nature. “The Seedling” is a concise yet meaningful poem that employs a seedling as a powerful symbol for human life and growth. The central theme centres on patience, perseverance and hope, suggesting that genuine growth takes time and often goes unnoticed by others. In the poem, Dunbar paints a vivid picture of a small seedling hidden beneath the soil. This seedling does not grow rapidly or draw attention to itself, but it is very much alive and brimming with potential. It patiently gathers strength in silence, and though external observers may see no evidence of progress, the seedling is steadily developing beneath the surface. At the right moment, it breaks through the soil, emerging strong and vibrant.

This imagery draws a beautiful comparison betweenthe seedling and human beings, particularly those who quietly endure challenges and cultivate their strength over time. The poem imparts a valuable lesson: true success is rarely instantaneous, and patience is essential for authentic growth.

Dunbar skillfully employs various poetic devices throughout the poem. The poem follows an ABAB rhyme scheme, with “seedling” rhyming with “talking” and “bed” rhyming with “said”. Similarly, “robust” rhymes with “moment”, “can” with “began”, and “day” with “way”. Symbolism plays a pivotal role, as the seedling represents human life and inner development. A seedling symbolises human potential and resilience. Light symbolises hope, success, and enlightenment. Soil/darkness symbolise life’s struggles. Vivid imagery allows readers to visualise the seed's hidden journey and gradual emergence. Alliteration is used in the words “planting, pushing, patiently”, where the repeated ‘p’ sound adds rhythm and makes the line more musical. Additionally, personification “pushing toward the light, “enriches the poem as the seedling is depicted as waiting and growing with patience.

The use of simple language and a calm tone contributes to the clarity and effectiveness of the message. I find “The Seedling” to be an uplifting poem that inspires hope and patience, especially during challenging times. Dunbar beautifully reminds us that quiet determination and perseverance will ultimately lead to success.

Phil Collins is a famous English singer, songwriter, and musician known for his meaningful and socially relevant songs. His song “Another Day in Paradise” highlights the harsh realities of modern society. The central theme of the song is social inequality and human indifference towards the poor and homeless. Through this song, the poet strongly criticises people who ignore the suffering of others while living in comfort. The song belongs to the genre of socially conscious lyrical song.

In the song, the poet describes the life of a homeless woman standing on the street, ignored by people who pass by without noticing her pain. She asks for help, but no one listens to her. People continue their daily routines, pretending that they do not see her suffering. The phrase “another day in paradise” is used ironically to highlight the contrast between the privileged and the poor, with the former enjoying comfortable lives and the latter enduring miserable conditions. The song urges listeners to open their eyes and hearts to the pain around them and to show compassion instead of indifference.

The song makes effective use of poetic devices. Irony is clearly seen in the title and the repeated line “another day in paradise,” which contrasts with the woman’s suffering. The simple and conversational language makes the song easily understandable and emotionally touching.

The story takes place during a local train

journey to Sulmona, where a group of passengers share their personal experiences related to the war. Among the passengers is a stout woman who is travelling with her husband. She is worried and anxious because her son has been sent to the war front. Other passengers also speak about their sons who are fighting in the war, and some have already lost their children. Though they talk calmly, their silent grief and suffering can be clearly felt. One man shocks everyone by saying that children belong to the nation, and parents should be proud if their sons die for the country. Through this simple train journey, Pirandello exposes the harsh reality and futility of war. As a reader, I felt the woman’s anxiety and helplessness, while her husband’s forced calm showed how people try to hide their pain. The other passengers discuss war casually, revealing the indifference and self-centred attitude of society. Some even speak as if war is necessary, showing how easily people accept violence without thinking about its human cost.

The emotional turning point of the story exposes the truth that parental love is universal. When the woman questions the idea that children belong to the nation, the emotional breakdown of a character shows that no belief or patriotism can suppress a parent’s grief. This scene made me realise how deeply war wounds the human heart. The story is highly relevant to present-day conditions, where wars continue and society often remains silent spectators. Pirandello’s “War” made me understand that war does not bring

honour or victory, but only pain, loss and emotional destruction. It urges readers to question war and choose humanity and peace over blind acceptance. 5. Parental love is one of the deepest and most powerful emotions experienced by human beings, and Luigi Pirandello’s short story War beautifully highlights its intensity. In the story, parents travelling in a train speak about their sons who have been sent to the war front. Though some of them try to appear proud and patriotic, their words cannot hide their inner pain and fear. The stout woman, who worries about her only son, clearly represents a mother’s unconditional love. Her anxiety and emotional outburst show that no idea of patriotism or sacrifice can reduce a parent’s suffering. When she questions the belief that children belong to the nation, the emotional breakdown of another parent proves that parental love is universal and unavoidable. A parent cannot divide love between family and country, because the bond with a child is personal and lifelong.

Even in the present world, parents continue to experience the same fear and helplessness when their children are in danger. Through War, Pirandello reminds us that parental love crosses all boundaries and remains stronger than war, ideology or national pride.

Character Sketch of the Stout Old Man Luigi Pirandello’s short story War presents the stout old man as a character who tries hard to control his grief with patience, reason and outward strength. At first, he appears calm, confident and firm in his views about war and sacrifice. During the discussion in the train, he strongly states that children belong to the nation and that parents should feel proud if their sons die for their country. His words give the impression that he has accepted his son’s death bravely and without complaint.

However, as the story progresses, the reader understands that this confidence is only a mask. The stout old man is actually a deeply wounded father who has lost his only son at the war front. His patriotic arguments are not heartless beliefs but a way to suppress his unbearable pain and to convince himself that his son’s death had meaning. He shows great self-control and patience, trying to appear strong before others, though his inner world is filled with sorrow.

The emotional turning point occurs when the stout woman questions his belief about sacrifice and asks whether he would truly feel proud if his own son were dead. This simple yet powerful question shatters his emotional barrier, and he breaks down completely, bursting into tears. This moment reveals his true self—a grieving parent whose love cannot be controlled by ideas of patriotism. Through the character of the stout old man, Pirandello highlights the universal nature of parental love and exposes the deep emotional scars left by war on innocent parents. 8.On hearing that his son has been chosen to be sent to the war front, the father in the story is overwhelmed with mixed emotions. Diary Entry 15 September 1915, Wednesday.

Today has been one of the most painful days of my life. I heard the news that my son has been chosen to be sent to the war front. My heart is heavy, and my hands tremble as I write these lines. I try to remain calm before others, but inside me there is a storm of fear, sorrow and helplessness.

Everyone speaks of war as duty and sacrifice, but how can a father think of such things when his only son’s life is in danger? I want to feel proud, yet my heart refuses to accept it. The thought of losing him haunts me. I imagine his smile, his voice, and I wonder whether I will ever see him again. I try to convince myself that he belongs to the nation, that his sacrifice will bring honour. Still, my heart cries out as a father. No words can reduce this pain. I realise that no idea of patriotism can replace a child’s life. Tonight, sleep escapes me. I pray silently for his safety and wish that this cruel war would end soon. All I want is my son back in my arms. Is that too much to ask?

‘ A Piece of String ‘ is a touching story written by Guy de Maupassant,a renowned French writer and a master of short story. In this psychological realistic short story, the writer portrays the harsh realities of rural French life and the destructive power of gossip. ‘A Piece of String, a realistic fiction develops through the mental conflicts of the protagonist, Huachecome. He is misunderstood and wrongly judged by the society. He dies as a victim of falsely accused by his fellow beings. Hauchecome, an old peasant of Goderville found a piece of string from the public square on a crowded market day. He took it as he believed that everything useful should be picked up. It was witnessed by his enemy Malandain, the harness maker. They were on bad terms with each other. He concealed the string in his trouser’s pocket as he felt shame to be seen thus by his enemy.

While enjoying the food at the tavern, he noticed the public crier’s announcement of the lost of a pocketbook containing five hundred francs and some business papers. A reward of twenty francs was also declared. After sometime, Hauchecome was taken to the Mayor’s office by the chief of the gendarmes. There in the Mayor’s office, he was questioned by the Mayor for falsely accusing of taking the pocketbook from the market square. He was shocked when he realised that it was Malandain who raised the allegation against him. He was confronted with Malandain. The Mayor questioned him and even searched him after the request by Malandain. He tried his level best to keep his self importance and pride. The Mayor discharged him as nothing was found on him. The people of Goderville laughed at him whenever he tried to prove his innocence. Even though the pocketbook was recovered, the people of Goderville continued their attitude against Hauchecome.

For proving his innocence, the poor peasant recounted his story of adventure to everyone. People had the air of joking while they listened. They did not seem convinced. He seemed to feel that remarks were being made behind his back. His last attempt for proving his innocence served another mental agony. A person in the tavern accused him of having the pocketbook returned by an accomplice. He tried to protest, but in vain. He returned home ashamed. Next day onwards he began to recount the adventure. Each time he added new reasons, more energetic protestations, more solemn oaths. No one believed him. Towards the end of December, he took to his bed. He died in the first days of January, and even in his last breath, he tried hard to claim his innocence.

Hauchecome is the protagonist of the short story A Piece of String written by Guy de Maupassant. The plot of this realistic short story develops through the conflicts inside and outside of the main character. The internal conflict within the protagonist and the conflicts between him and the society are also well portrayed in the story. Hauchecome is an innocent, pride and simple peasant in the town of Goderville. He is a typical French peasant who believes that everything useful should be picked up even if it is a piece of string. His act of taking a simple piece of string ultimately leads to his death. This trivial act is misjudged by his enemy Malandain, a harness maker which destroys Hauchecome’s good will among the people of Goderville. He possesses a strong sense of self importance. He is ashamed to be seen by Malandain taking the piece of string. He immediately tries to hide it.

He argues before the Mayor for suspecting him for taking the pocketbook as per the lies of Malandain. He is so simple that he repeatedly tries to prove his innocence which creates suspicion in the minds of people. He always insists that he only picks up the piece of string. The allegation of the horse dealer that he hands over the pocketbook by using an accomplice makes him mentally weak. Even in his deathbed, he tries to prove his innocence. Hauchecome is deeply concerned with his good will. He is falsely accused and misjudged by the society. He is a victim of social cruelty. He recounts his adventure to everyone, but the people of Goderville don’t seem to believe his words. Their rumours, gossips and mockery lead to the death of a simple peasant who gives more importance to his pride and conscience. He values his reputation and honesty more than anything.

At the age of 17, Nick began motivational speaking, transforming his disability into a powerful platform to inspire others.

He has since become a globally renowned inspirational _ Speaker, travelling to over 60 countries and founding the NGO Life without Limbs . He emphasises that fear is the greatest disability, not physical impairment, and advocates that life's challenges can be transformed into strengths. UNIT 4 WOODLAND WHISPERS 1. Shakuntalam : At a glance Kalidasa’s play Shakuntalam beautifully portrays the way our ancestors lived in close harmony with nature. It reminds us that breaking this bond with nature leads to destruction, while peaceful coexistence ensures balance and well-being. In Shakuntalam, Kalidasa shows that humans can live in harmony with nature through love, care, and respect. The hermitage is a peaceful place where plants and animals are treated like family members. The play teaches that when humans protect nature, nature, in turn, supports and nurtures human life.

The play opens with King Dushyanta pursuing a deer in the forest in his chariot. As he admires the grace and beauty of the animal, he prepares to shoot it. At that moment, a voice cautions him against killing the deer. Two hermits soon appear and explain that the deer belongs to their hermitage and is under their protection. They gently remind the king that weapons are meant to defend the innocent, not to harm the helpless. Respecting their wisdom, the king lowers his bow and returns the arrow to his quiver. Pleased with his conduct, the hermits bless him and invite him to visit Sage Kanva’s hermitage, where his foster daughter Shakuntala looks after the place in his absence.

When Dushyanta arrives at the hermitage, he is deeply impressed by the calm and sacred atmosphere. He observes parrots dropping grains of rice, oil-stained pounding stones lying around, and gentle deer roaming freely without fear. Realising the serenity of the place, the king waits silently so as not to disturb its peace. Soon, he notices Shakuntala along with her friends, Anasuya and Priyamvada, watering the plants. They care for the trees lovingly, treating them like members of their own family. They compare Shakuntala to a delicate jasmine creeper and delight in the natural beauty around them. The king is instantly captivated by Shakuntala’s grace, purity, and simplicity.

As Shakuntala bends down to water a creeper, a bee begins to hover around her, frightening her. Her friends teasingly suggest that she call upon King Dushyanta, the guardian of the hermitage, to protect her from the bee. The hermitage is shown as a place where human life, plants, and animals exist in perfect harmony, and nature is treated with love and reverence. Through this, the play suggests that human happiness and moral living are closely linked to respect for the natural world. William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet, dramatist, and one of the central figures of 20th-century literature. Yeats’s writing style is distinguished by musical language, symbolic imagery, and a fusion of the mystical with the real. His poem “The Wild Swans at Coole” is a gentle, reflective piece in which the poet observes a group of swans on an autumn evening. The calm, beautiful setting makes him think deeply about change, ageing, and the passage of time. The main theme of the poem is the contrast between the poet’s ageing and the unchanging, youthful energy of the swans. While Yeats feels the effects of time on his own life—tiredness, loneliness, and the awareness that things have changed—the swans remain graceful, full of life, and constant in their companionship. The poem expresses a quiet sadness as well as admiration for the swans’ beauty and freedom. It reminds us that nature can remain eternal even as human life changes.

The poem opens with a picturesque description of the trees in their autumn beauty, the dry woodlands and the lake water mirroring the sky. The swans, those ‘brilliant creatures’ ‘mysterious and beautiful,’ paddling in the cold companionable streams or climbing the air are very much a part of nature. The depiction of the scenic beauty of the park and the graceful elegance of the swans inspire readers to value nature. The swans seem to represent lasting youth and beauty. They do not appear to be affected by the passage of time. They are not seen to yield to the onset of old- age. Instead, they ‘paddle’ in the ‘streams’, ‘unwearied’, ‘lover by lover’. As the poet notes,‘Their hearts have not grown old.’ The swans, unlike us, are majestic. They drift on the still water, climb the air, painting the sky with the bell beat of their wings and fly away before the poet realises they are gone. The poem is rich in images of youth and old- age.

The trees in their autumn beauty, the dry woodland paths and the twilight represent old- age. In contrast, the still sky could represent the seemingly-eternal youthful glory of the swans. They do not seem to grow old. They move about unwearied, lover by lover, paddling along the streams. The poet believes that this is because ‘their hearts have not grown old.’ ‘The bell-beat of the wings’, ‘trod with lighter tread’, ‘they paddle in the field’, ‘companionable streams or climb the air’ etc are some of the examples of alliteration. ‘And scatter wheeling in great broken rings’ is an example of assonance. Symbolism is also important: the mirror symbolises truth, while candles and the moon symbolise illusion and false comfort.

In brief, the poem presents a woman who depends on the mirror to understand her identity.
